evidence_quotes.quote: The service level provided by a new or improved water supply involves a combination of factors, including the quantity and quality of the water, the amount of time needed to collect water, and the reliability of the system.

For every scheme, an organization such as a water committee is needed to manage collection of charges from users, to initiate repair and maintenance activities, to manage payments for maintenance services, and to procure spare parts.
The Project's model evaluates and compares the costs of alternative pumping technologies and types of water supply systems.

In order to evaluate rural water supply (RWS) projects, the Project has devised a simple analytical tool, based on traditional cost/benefit analysis. The model can be used to compare the service levels, costs and benefits of alternative RWS systems.

In comparing different RWS options, the model first determines the optimum handpumps and standpipe systems by computing the annualized costs and benefits of providing different numbers of handpumps or standpipes and choosing the number of handpumps or standpipes that provides the greatest net benefit.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community and household drinking-water supply service levels (handpumps, standpipes, and yard taps), discussing water quantity, quality, collection time, and reliability.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the paper does not examine any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure); instead, its analytical model compares physical pumping technologies and delivery options based on engineering and economic parameters (population, pumping lift, well cost, and value of time). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, Section 2.2(iii)-(iv) briefly mentions in general background prose that water committees, Village Level Operation and Maintenance (VLOM), and community or government financing are needed for project sustainability, but no legal, administrative, institutional, or governance factor is actually analysed or modelled as an exposure, and even if those background remarks were treated as satisfying plain Criterion 2, the paper would still be excluded for lacking empirical evidence (c3).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains no empirical primary data, no empirical case study, and no systematic empirical synthesis. Aside from a brief background mention that UNDP/World Bank field trials of handpumps took place earlier in the program, the paper presents a theoretical/analytical cost-benefit planning model illustrated on a hypothetical prototype village. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses service-level concepts (quantity, collection time, reliability) conceptually, but the model outputs are simulated least-cost pumping thresholds and optimum net economic benefit equilibriums for a hypothetical prototype village rather than measured empirical access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: No empirical population, sample, legal/governance exposure, or empirical study design can be identified because the analysis is a deterministic cost-benefit simulation for a hypothetical prototype village.

study_design: Analytical cost-benefit planning model / non-empirical technical-economic overview
exposure: Alternative rural water supply technologies and delivery systems (handpumps, standpipes, yard taps; manual, solar, diesel, and electric pumps) modelled across physical and economic parameters (population, water volume, pumping lift, well cost, and value of collection time)
outcome: Simulated annualized costs and optimum net economic benefit equilibriums for selecting rural water supply technologies in a hypothetical prototype village
rationale: This 1989 World Bank/UNDP paper presents an analytical cost-benefit planning model and technical-economic overview for selecting groundwater pumping technologies (manual handpumps, solar, diesel, electric) and service options (handpumps, standpipes, yard taps) in a hypothetical prototype village. It contains no primary empirical data, empirical sample, or systematic empirical synthesis (excluded as E05: No empirical evidence), and it also examines engineering/economic technology choice rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing water access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2.
